title: Your child tells you something frightening
lede: Bullying, self-harm, a message they should not have received, drugs, an assault, a pregnancy, a debt to someone older. They have finally said it and they are watching your face to see what happens next.

blocks.text: Bullying, self-harm, a message they should not have received, drugs, an assault, a pregnancy, a debt to someone older. They have finally said it and they are watching your face to see what happens next.

items: Your first three seconds determine whether they ever tell you anything again. Everything else in this situation is recoverable; that is not.
They have already spent days or weeks deciding whether to tell you, and they have rehearsed your worst reaction.
The urge to act immediately — phone the school, confront the parent, remove the phone — is often about your own distress and can make them regret disclosing.
They usually need to keep some control over what happens next. Total removal of agency is why children stop disclosing.

items.move: Control your face and thank them
items.detail: Whatever it is. Calm and warm, not shocked or furious. This is the whole hinge.

items.move: Let them tell it fully before you respond
items.detail: No interrogation, no interruption, no leading questions. Just "and then what happened?"
"I believe you." "You are not in trouble." "We will sort this together."

items.move: Ask what they want to happen
items.detail: Then be honest about what has to happen anyway. Involving them in the plan is what preserves the relationship.

items.move: Write down what they said, in their words
items.detail: Especially if it involves another person, a crime, or a safeguarding issue. Contemporaneous notes matter enormously later.

items.move: Get the right help within days
items.detail: School safeguarding lead, doctor, police, or a specialist service depending on what it is. Do not carry a serious disclosure alone.

items.say: "Thank you for telling me. That took guts. You are not in trouble and I am not angry with you."
"Take your time. Start wherever you want and tell me all of it — I can handle it."
"Here is what I think has to happen and why. What part of that worries you most? Let us work out how to do it."

items.when: If they ask you to keep it secret
items.say: "I will not tell anyone who does not need to know. I might need one adult who can actually help — and I will tell you before I do it."

items: Anger, even at the other person, in the first conversation. They cannot separate it from anger at them.
"Why did you not tell me sooner?" It punishes the disclosure you just received.
Confiscating the phone or the internet as a first move. It reads as punishment and cuts their support network.
Confronting another child's parents in the heat of it.
Promising absolute secrecy you cannot keep.
Check in briefly and regularly without making it the only subject you discuss.
Keep the routine going. Predictability is stabilising for children under stress.
Get support for yourself separately. Do not process your fear in front of them.
Tell them explicitly, once things settle, that telling you was the right call. It builds the channel for next time.

limit: If there is sexual abuse, exploitation, grooming, physical injury, or a risk to their life, contact the police or a child-protection service today. Do not investigate it yourself and do not confront a suspected abuser — it can destroy evidence and increase risk.
